evidence: Full CDIAL distinguishes masculine trayaḥ/trāyaḥ from neuter trīṇi. The Bhil survey ṭiṇ has the i vowel and final nasal of section 3, alongside Prakrit tiṇṇi, Gujarati traṇ and Marathi/Hindi tīn; it cannot be assigned to the a-vowel sections from the English numeral alone. Source retroflex onset and final ṇ are retained. The family link does not select a particular modern donor.

CDIAL karṇa gives Prakrit kaṇṇa and Gujarati/Marathi/Hindi kān “ear”, with widespread nasal place variants across its reflexes. The selected neighbouring Bhil attestations retain the same kā- plus nasal body-part stem; their word-final ŋ is explicitly present in the original survey transcription, not silently normalized to n. This is a family assignment; the phonetic value/place of the final nasal remains as transcribed.

Turner explicitly places Lahnda gā̃ (plural gãī) and Awankari gā̃ (plural gāī̃) under section 3 gāvī. The Pahari-Pothwari Lahndic survey has the same contracted nasalized cow form. This uses the same-region comparator, not nasalization alone: identical-looking Punjabi gā̃ is listed in section 2, so Gujari and Haryanvi homographs are not included.

CDIAL sarpa gives Prakrit sappa, Lahnda/Punjabi sapp and explicitly Awankari sap “snake”. The survey sapʰ matches that short-vowel, retained-stop family; final release aspiration is preserved as recorded and does not motivate a distinct etymon. These are simple responses, without the material of the feminine sarpiṇī or young-snake derivatives.

Full kim explicitly records Maiya gī “what”, beside Gawri kī and Phalura ga. The selected Indus Kohistani/Maiya responses match that same-language comparator and require no added suffix or competing ka-stem analysis.
